holidays.name: Howl at the Moon Night
holidays.description: Step outside after dark, tip your head back and let out your wildest wolf impression. The night is for unleashing your inner wolf, coyote or very dramatic dog. Neighbors are welcome to join in, or to wonder what is going on.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It has become a cheerful excuse to be loud and silly under the night sky.
holidays.funFact: Wolves don't howl because of the moon. They howl to communicate with their pack and mark territory. Howling at the moon is a myth, but it's a fun one.

holidays.name: National Chicken Fried Steak Day
holidays.description: This day honors a comfort-food classic: a tenderized steak that is breaded, fried until crisp and golden, and smothered in peppery cream gravy. It's a plate of pure Southern-style indulgence. Today is a day to skip the salad.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food holiday of unclear origin. The dish is widely tied to the American South and Southwest, where German and Austrian immigrants' schnitzel traditions are thought to have shaped it.
holidays.funFact: Chicken fried steak contains no chicken. The name comes from cooking the beef the way you would fry chicken.

holidays.name: National Mule Day
holidays.description: This is a salute to the hardworking, clever and famously stubborn mule. Mules are the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse. They have long been prized for their strength, endurance and sure-footedness.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It recognizes the long history of mules as farm and pack animals.
holidays.funFact: Mules are almost always sterile, so breeders have to cross a donkey and a horse every time to make a new one.
